title: Harness Engineering - Awesome Security & AI Research
description: How to build agent and coding harnesses that cost less, run faster, fail less and get more correct work done: measured results from papers, lab and practitioner engineering blogs, with the standing claims they support.

subcategories.name: Cost efficiency
subcategories.scope: Token use and spend - prompt caching, context budgets, cheaper subagents and model routing, keeping tool output out of context, cost per task.

subcategories.name: Work efficiency
subcategories.scope: More correct work per hour - planning and spec steps, task decomposition, delegation, parallel agents, verification loops, measured productivity.

subcategories.name: Speed and latency
subcategories.scope: Wall-clock time per task, agent-loop and tool latency, parallel and speculative tool calls, cache reuse for speed.

subcategories.name: Reliability and recovery
subcategories.scope: Getting runs to finish correctly - error recovery, loop and stall detection, long-horizon drift, failure taxonomies, tracing, run-to-run variance.

subcategories.name: Context and memory
subcategories.scope: What the model sees - context engineering, compaction, agent memory, retrieval for agents, long-context failure modes.

subcategories.name: Tools and interfaces
subcategories.scope: How the harness exposes actions - tool design and descriptions, schemas and structured output, skills, MCP servers built for agents, sandboxes as tools.

subcategories.name: Orchestration and multi-agent
subcategories.scope: How work is split across agents and turns - subagents, planners, multi-agent coordination, long-running and background agents.

subcategories.name: Evaluating harnesses
subcategories.scope: Measuring a harness rather than a model - harness ablations, agent benchmarks, trajectory analysis, eval-to-production gaps.

subcategories.name: Harness design
subcategories.scope: Everything else about building the agent loop itself - architecture, prompts, control flow, autonomy and approval design.

claims.title: Send simple subagent jobs to a cheaper model
claims.statement: Anthropic's docs recommend routing simple subagent jobs to a cheaper model such as Haiku, and Aider's architect/editor split shows a reasoning model can pair with a weaker editor without losing quality.
claims.guidance: Set Haiku-class models on search and summarizing subagents; keep the top model for the lead.

claims.title: Compact near the context limit; reset only if the model needs it
claims.statement: A harness should compact long sessions automatically, and add hard context resets only for models that wrap up early near the limit.
claims.guidance: Enable auto-compaction first; test whether resets still help on your current model.

claims.title: Return short tool responses and distilled subagent summaries
claims.statement: A harness that makes tools return concise fields, and subagents return condensed summaries (often 1,000-2,000 tokens), keeps the main context smaller; Anthropic's example used about a third of the tokens.
claims.guidance: Offer a concise response format on tools and cap subagent reports.

claims.title: Harness choice alone can double an agent's cost
claims.statement: On the same model and task, the harness alone changed cost up to about 2x at similar accuracy, and coding agents' first call ranges from about 1.9k to 32k input tokens.
claims.guidance: Measure what your harness spends per task (fixed prompt and tool schemas, plus re-reading context) and cut what does not change outcomes before you switch models.

claims.title: Keep intermediate tool results out of the model context
claims.statement: In Anthropic's own measurement, processing tool output in code and passing only results to the model cut average tokens by 37% on complex research tasks.
claims.guidance: Run bulk filtering in a code sandbox or write long output to a file and let the agent grep it.

claims.title: Learn per-repo cost controls from past coding agent runs
claims.statement: A controller that learns from earlier runs in the same repository which tools to prune, which short notes to inject and when to stop unproductive failure loops cut coding-agent cost by 18-31% on SWE-Bench with comparable task success.
claims.guidance: Log where tokens go across runs in one repo; prune tools the repo never uses, add short notes for operations the agent keeps rediscovering, and guard against loops that keep failing the same way while letting recoverable ones continue.

claims.title: Load tool definitions on demand, not all at start
claims.statement: Vendors report that loading tool definitions only when needed cut tokens by 47% (Cursor A/B test, runs that called an MCP tool) to 85% (Anthropic Tool Search); Anthropic's 98.7% is a single worked example.
claims.guidance: Expose tool names only, and fetch a tool's schema when the task needs it.

claims.title: Treat multi-agent as a token multiplier; use it where breadth pays
claims.statement: A harness should use multi-agent runs only for breadth-first tasks, because they use about 15 times the tokens of chat.
claims.guidance: Default to one agent; spawn parallel subagents only for independent, high-value branches and track tokens per run.

claims.title: Use one-hour cache markers when sessions pause over five minutes
claims.statement: Harnesses that write 5-minute prompt-cache markers re-buy their whole context after an idle gap longer than five minutes, while harnesses with 1-hour markers kept about 86% cache hits after a 390-second pause.
claims.guidance: For interactive sessions where people or tools often pause for more than five minutes, cache the stable prefix with the 1-hour TTL; keep 5-minute caching for tight automated loops.

claims.title: Prefer the simplest pipeline that solves the task
claims.statement: A harness should start with a simple fixed workflow, since in 2024 the non-agentic Agentless pipeline scored highest among open-source agents on SWE-bench Lite (32.00%) at $0.70 per task, in the authors' own evaluation.
claims.guidance: Add agent loops, tools or subagents only after a simpler version fails on your evals.

claims.title: Keep the prompt prefix stable so cache reads dominate
claims.statement: A harness that keeps its context append-only and its prefix stable gets cached input at roughly a tenth of the uncached price.
claims.guidance: Never edit earlier turns or reorder the system prompt/tools mid-session; only append.

claims.title: Measure speedups with repeated trials, not impressions
claims.statement: A harness team should judge work efficiency with repeated-trial evals or timed studies, since in METR's early-2025 study developers believed AI sped them up while it slowed them down.
claims.guidance: Track time-to-merged-change and pass rate over multiple trials per task before claiming a gain.

claims.title: Parallelize independent reads; keep writes single-threaded
claims.statement: A harness should fan out parallel subagents for independent research but keep code-writing in one context, since Cognition argues parallel writers act on conflicting assumptions.
claims.guidance: Parallelize search and review; serialize edits through one agent that holds the shared context.

claims.title: Persist a feature list and progress log across sessions
claims.statement: A harness for long tasks should write a structured feature list and progress file so each new session can resume instead of one-shotting the app.
claims.guidance: Have an initializer write a JSON feature list, init script and progress file; work one feature per session.

claims.title: Re-test harness scaffolding whenever the model changes
claims.statement: A harness should treat each component as an assumption about model weakness, stress-test it on each model upgrade, and remove it if it is no longer needed.
claims.guidance: Ablate one component at a time on each model upgrade and keep only what moves your eval.

claims.title: Split generating from evaluating with a separate grader
claims.statement: A separate evaluator scoring against explicit criteria was part of a three-agent harness that cost over 20x a solo run and, in the author's judgment on one prompt, produced visibly better output.
claims.guidance: Write gradable criteria and run a fresh-context reviewer; keep it for tasks where quality justifies the spend.

claims.title: Verify end-to-end as a user, not only with unit tests
claims.statement: A harness should make the agent exercise the running app (browser automation) before marking work done, since unit tests and curl miss broken features.
claims.guidance: Require a browser-driven check or /verify-style step before a task is marked complete.

claims.title: Few-shot prompting is brittle to formatting choices
claims.statement: Few-shot prompting accuracy is highly sensitive to example ordering, whitespace, and demarcation choices, in ways that look like model regressions if not controlled for.
claims.guidance: Freeze prompt formatting when evaluating model changes.

claims.title: Hybrid BM25 + vector search beats pure vector retrieval
claims.statement: Hybrid search (BM25 + dense vectors) outperforms pure vector retrieval on most enterprise/technical corpora, because vector embeddings underweight exact term matches that carry high signal.
claims.guidance: Default to hybrid retrieval unless you've measured that pure-vector wins on your specific corpus.

claims.title: Long context windows don't remove the need for retrieval
claims.statement: Long-context models do not eliminate the need for retrieval: they exhibit lost-in-the-middle effects, cost grows linearly with context size, and per-token attention drops on distant tokens.
claims.guidance: Retrieval + a short, relevant context still beats stuffing a long context on cost, latency, and accuracy for most tasks.

claims.title: Retrieval quality dominates generator quality in RAG
claims.statement: In production RAG systems, retrieval quality dominates generation quality as a determinant of end-task accuracy; larger models cannot compensate for a bad retriever.
claims.guidance: Invest in retrieval evals (recall@k, reranker quality) before spending on bigger generator models.

claims.title: System prompts are load-bearing config — version them like code
claims.statement: Production system prompts are load-bearing configuration and should be version-controlled, code-reviewed, and evaluated on regression suites.
claims.guidance: Store prompts in the same repo as the code that calls them. Run eval on every prompt change and every model change.

claims.title: Constrained decoding wins for structured output, not TOON
claims.statement: For structured model OUTPUT, constrained decoding gives the lowest token usage and plain JSON generation the best accuracy — token-optimized notations do not win here.
claims.guidance: Split the decision by direction. Use a token-optimized notation for what you feed in; use constrained decoding (or plain JSON) for what you ask the model to emit.

claims.title: Model upgrades can regress on non-native tool schemas
claims.statement: A newer SOTA model can be WORSE at your harness's custom tool schema than its older siblings — Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 invented fields in a third-party edit tool that older models got right — plausibly because RL training tuned them to their own harness's tools.
claims.guidance: Match your harness's tool schemas to what the target model was trained on — Claude on str-replace-style edits, OpenAI on apply_patch — and offer a model-matched edit tool in multi-model harnesses. Re-run tool-calling evals on every model upgrade.

claims.title: TOON beats JSON on input-side token cost
claims.statement: For large uniform arrays, TOON serializes to 30-60% fewer input tokens than JSON at comparable retrieval accuracy.
claims.guidance: Use TOON for the big uniform/tabular payloads you feed INTO the model (tool results, row sets, retrieved records). Keep JSON where data is deeply nested or irregular.

claims.title: Auto-evolved harness gains are mostly overfitting
claims.statement: Gains from automatically evolving an agent harness (prompts, skills, tools, orchestration around a fixed model) are mostly search-set overfitting and extra inference compute: across 21 settings with significant gains, those two explained 54% and 14% of the gain on average, search-set gains often failed to transfer to held-out tasks, and a validation split did not prevent the overfitting.
claims.guidance: Accept an auto-evolved harness change only on its delta over a held-out task set the optimizer never saw, measured at matched inference budget; don't trust search-set or validation-set improvement.

claims.title: SWE-bench scores don't predict production task performance
claims.statement: SWE-bench scores do not linearly predict agent performance on production engineering tasks; the benchmark rewards a specific style of small-diff bug-fix.
claims.guidance: Treat SWE-bench as one data point, not a complete picture. Build in-house evals on your task mix.

claims.title: An agent's stated lean steers expert judgment calls
claims.statement: When an agent states a preference on an open judgment call, experts mostly follow it: in Anthropic's randomized study analysts matched a coin-flip-assigned agent lean 86% of the time versus about 50% expected with no influence, often reusing the agent's arguments without crediting it.
claims.guidance: At human decision points in a harness, have the agent present the strongest case for each option and capture the human's own preference before the agent states its lean; do not rely on the human's self-report to judge whether they were steered.

claims.title: Single-turn CoT gains don't transfer to multi-turn tasks
claims.statement: Single-turn benchmark gains, including from chain-of-thought reasoning, do not reliably carry over to multi-turn agent tasks: top models lose about 39% from single- to multi-turn settings, and reasoning models degrade the same way.
claims.guidance: Evaluate agents on the multi-turn task, not a single-turn proxy.

claims.title: Coding agents hallucinate plausible but nonexistent APIs
claims.statement: Coding assistants generate calls to functions and APIs that do not exist in the target library or version — plausible spelling, correct-looking signature, no runtime existence.
claims.guidance: Any LLM-suggested import or API call must be validated against the actual library documentation for the pinned version.

claims.title: Diff review catches more LLM-introduced defects than full-file review
claims.statement: Reviewing an LLM's proposed change as a diff catches more defects than reviewing the resulting full file.
claims.guidance: Prefer tools that present LLM changes as diffs. Reviewer must sign off on the specific lines that changed.

claims.title: Lean tool sets and reasoning-first prompts work best
claims.statement: Coding-agent harnesses work better with few distinct tools and a lean system prompt of reasoning rather than rules.
claims.guidance: Keep the tool count small and the tools clearly distinct; write the system prompt as reasoning rather than rule lists; grow your eval suite out of real incidents; gate dangerous actions with a context-aware permission classifier rather than a static allowlist.

claims.title: Too many tools degrade agent tool-selection accuracy
claims.statement: Showing an agent more candidate tools than the task needs degrades tool-selection accuracy: short, query-adapted tool lists select better than a fixed longer list (93.1% vs 87.1% on BFCL with Claude Sonnet 4.6).
claims.guidance: Curate the tool set. Retire tools whose calls the eval suite shows agents get wrong more than they get right.

items.title: Hugging Face guide shows how to build and validate an agentic evaluation
items.summary: Before you trust an agent eval, run a do-nothing agent and a shortcut solution against the grader, and read the traces.
items.content_text: The guide walks through eight steps of building an agentic evaluation by adapting a Terminal-Bench task for fitting peaks in Raman spectra. The authors tested the grader with a do-nothing agent and a shortcut script that skips the fitting; the shortcut returned the expected ratio on all eight tasks, so a ratio-only check would have passed it, and they added checks on each fitted peak. Reading traces showed most failures were early stops, not bad fits.

_stream.takeaway: Before you trust an agent eval, run a do-nothing agent and a shortcut solution against the grader, and read the traces.

action.title: Test every grader with a null agent and a shortcut solution
action.detail: Before running models, confirm the reference solution passes, a do-nothing agent fails, and a script that skips the required work fails; then report pass^k as well as pass@k.

items.title: Google adds Tool Retrieval to the Gemini API to defer tool schemas
items.summary: Deferring tool schemas is now a built-in API feature, so large tool libraries need not be sent in full on every request.
items.content_text: Google launched Tool Retrieval in preview in the Gemini Interactions API. You add a tool_search tool and mark tools with defer_loading set to true. The model still sees each deferred tool's name and description, but the full parameter schemas load only when the model asks for them. Google says this cuts input tokens and latency and helps tool selection stay accurate as the tool list grows, and that it works with Gemini 3.6 and later models.

_stream.takeaway: Deferring tool schemas is now a built-in API feature, so large tool libraries need not be sent in full on every request.

action.title: Defer tool schemas for large tool libraries
action.detail: If your agent carries dozens of tools, keep names and one-line descriptions in context and load full parameter schemas only when a tool is chosen. In the Gemini Interactions API add a tool_search tool and set defer_loading true on the tools to hold back; it is in preview and needs Gemini 3.6 or later. Measure input tokens and tool-selection accuracy before and after, since the post reports no numbers in the text read.

items.title: Eugene Yan finds graders failed valid work in eight of twelve evals
items.summary: Read a benchmark score as a model-plus-harness-plus-grader result, and audit the grader before trusting the ranking.
items.content_text: Eugene Yan tears down twelve public agent benchmarks. In eight of them, audits or issue reports found graders rejecting valid work, and some passed wrong work. He argues for reliability metrics such as pass^k, for human attention over dollar cost, and for testing models in your own harness.

_stream.takeaway: Read a benchmark score as a model-plus-harness-plus-grader result, and audit the grader before trusting the ranking.

action.title: Audit your eval graders and report pass^k
action.detail: Add a do-nothing agent and an adversarial agent as negative tests, review tasks that several strong models fail the same way, run each task k times and report pass^k next to average pass rate, and score models inside your own harness.

items.title: UK AISI releases Transect to review long agent evaluation transcripts
items.summary: When you review agent eval runs, keep judge labels linked to transcript evidence and look at where judges disagree.
items.content_text: A final eval score hides what agents tried, where they got stuck and how the setup shaped their work. Transect is an open-source package built on Inspect Scout. It uses LLM judges to label stretches of a transcript and shows labels, token use and events on one timeline linked back to the source passages.

_stream.takeaway: When you review agent eval runs, keep judge labels linked to transcript evidence and look at where judges disagree.

action.title: Try Transect on your long agent eval transcripts
action.detail: Supply a transcript, the task context and your own activity categories (for example experiment design, coding, analysis). Use repeated or multiple judge models, check disagreements first, and export the tables for further analysis.

items.title: Claude Code team explains how it verifies agent-written code at scale
items.summary: Treat the verification layer as a system of its own: run the real app, keep the checks out of reach of the change, and measure the checks against past incidents.
items.content_text: The Claude Code team says about 90% of its code is written and reviewed by Claude, so verification loops are what let one person run many agents in parallel. The post recommends end-to-end, property and differential tests, a verify skill that boots and drives the app, and review gates that the change under review cannot edit. It also covers rolling out new gates in observe mode and turning missed bugs into review rules.

_stream.takeaway: Treat the verification layer as a system of its own: run the real app, keep the checks out of reach of the change, and measure the checks against past incidents.

action.title: Add a verify skill and an observe-mode commit gate
action.detail: Create a .claude/skills/verify skill next to the code that boots the app and drives it (browser, simulator or local service). Load review rules (such as REVIEW.md) from the default branch only. Add a commit gate with off, observe and enforce modes, stamp each commit with how it was verified (including 'none'), and let a commit through after two blocks so the agent is not stuck.

items.title: Microsoft finds 8% of coding sessions account for 44% of costs
items.summary: If you run long coding agent sessions, measure what compaction costs you and consider building summaries ahead of time in the background.
items.content_text: This digest's most practitioner-relevant item is a Microsoft study of 13.5 million coding agent sessions: fewer than 8% needed context compaction, yet those sessions made up 44% of total AI processing costs. The researchers released COMPACTIONBENCH to evaluate compaction and APEC, a method that prepares summaries in the background, which cut costs by up to 25.4% and execution time by 9.6%.

_stream.takeaway: If you run long coding agent sessions, measure what compaction costs you and consider building summaries ahead of time in the background.

action.title: Measure compaction cost share and try background summarization
action.detail: Log which sessions trigger compaction and what share of total tokens and cost they use. Then test a background summarizer that builds a running summary while the agent works, and swap it in at the threshold instead of pausing for a synchronous summary. Compare task success, cost and wall-clock time against the current method.

items.title: York University's FlowPlan cuts Claude Code tokens by planning edits first
items.summary: Replacing post-edit re-reading and re-testing with a stated plan cut coding agent tokens with no significant loss in fix rate.
items.content_text: FlowPlan has a coding agent localize the fault, state its intended change as a delta on per-function control-flow or data-flow graphs, and then check the actual change against that plan. On SWE-bench Pro, SWE-bench Verified and SecBench with Claude Code on Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5, resolution rate did not change significantly while token use fell in every setting, to as low as about a third of baseline. The baseline spent 3.7 million tokens per issue, 98% of them cache reads.

_stream.takeaway: Replacing post-edit re-reading and re-testing with a stated plan cut coding agent tokens with no significant loss in fix rate.

action.title: Add a stated-plan check before edits
action.detail: For bug-fix tasks, have the agent write down which functions it will change and how before editing, then check the diff against that plan instead of re-reading files and rerunning the full suite after each edit. Track turns and cache-read tokens per resolved issue.

items.title: UC Berkeley finds harness overhead can double agent cost at similar accuracy
items.summary: Measure how much of your agent spend is context rereads and harness overhead before tuning anything else.
items.content_text: UC Berkeley researchers profiled Claude Code, Codex and a plain ReAct harness on SWE-bench, SWE-bench Pro and Terminal-Bench 2 across five models. Harness choices barely moved accuracy but changed cost by up to 2.6x, and rereading existing context was the largest cost even with caching. Their interposition layer, Agency, applied fixes such as compacting tool output, batching tool calls and metadata-assisted search to unmodified harnesses and cut cost by up to 35% without losing accuracy.

_stream.source: UC Berkeley Sky Lab (Park et al.)
_stream.takeaway: Measure how much of your agent spend is context rereads and harness overhead before tuning anything else.

action.title: Audit fixed overhead, then batch tool calls
action.detail: Log input tokens per turn split into system prompt, tool schemas, cached history and new content for a week of real sessions. Cut always-on instructions and unused tool schemas, add a system-prompt line asking the model to batch independent reads into one turn, and compare cost per completed task before and after.

items.title: Token-Goat hooks coding agents to cut repeat reads and bulky tool output
items.summary: Most agent token waste is repeat reads and noisy tool output, which hooks can trim without changing the model.
items.content_text: Token-Goat is a hook layer for Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI and other agents that answers repeat file reads with a pointer, returns single symbols instead of whole files, strips build and test logs to failures, shrinks screenshots and caches skill loads. It also wraps every fetched page and tool result in an untrusted-content fence. Its savings figures (40 to 90% session cost) are self-reported, not independently benchmarked.

_stream.takeaway: Most agent token waste is repeat reads and noisy tool output, which hooks can trim without changing the model.

action.title: Deduplicate repeat reads and trim tool logs in hooks
action.detail: Add PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks that answer a re-read of an unchanged file with a pointer, strip passing tests and progress bars from build and test output, and downscale screenshots before they reach the model. Measure cost per task before and after rather than trusting the author's savings figures. A third-party hook sees every tool call, so review its code before installing it.

items.title: Researchers find agents keep accuracy with short, frequently compacted contexts
items.summary: Short, frequently compacted contexts kept accuracy here; on hosted APIs, test that against the cache hits each compaction gives up.
items.content_text: This paper argues that generating later tokens in a long context costs more than earlier ones, by up to 7x on frontier open-weight models, and tests whether agents need long context at all. With Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol, frequent compaction and reading long inputs selectively as stored documents kept task accuracy largely intact on long-horizon and long-input tasks. It also proposes semantic state space models, which would need a trained model.

_stream.takeaway: Short, frequently compacted contexts kept accuracy here; on hosted APIs, test that against the cache hits each compaction gives up.

action.title: Test frequent compaction against your cache savings
action.detail: Run the same task set with compaction at the context limit, at a lower threshold, and with long inputs moved to files the agent reads on demand. Compare accuracy and total cost including cache writes, since each compaction rewrites the prefix and loses cache hits.

items.title: OpenAI finds agents score worse on safety evals than in production
items.summary: Agent safety eval scores can swing on the model's guess about what is being tested, so builders should compare eval results against matched production traces and design evals whose objective is hard to infer.
items.content_text: OpenAI compared six models on its Respecting Warnings agent safety eval against matched decisions from real Codex production logs. Every model did worse in the eval, by 10.2 to 37.4 percentage points. The gap tracked how often a model guessed the wrong test objective, for example treating a real warning as a prompt injection to ignore. In an intervention on one model (GPT-6.1 Sol), stating the correct objective raised eval success to 91.6% and stating the wrong one cut it to 17.6%, while just saying 'this is an evaluation' changed nothing.

_stream.takeaway: Agent safety eval scores can swing on the model's guess about what is being tested, so builders should compare eval results against matched production traces and design evals whose objective is hard to infer.

action.title: Track the eval-to-production gap and objective guesses in agent safety evals
action.detail: For each agent safety eval you run, classify the reasoning traces for (a) statements that this is a test and (b) guesses about what is being tested, using two separate rubrics. Report success separately for rollouts with correct and wrong objective guesses. Where you have production logs, pick matched production decisions based only on the context before the decision, grade them with the same rubric, and track the gap per model. Rewrite eval cases where the 'correct' behavior can be inferred from surface cues, or where a warning looks like a prompt-injection test.

items.title: Legora evaluates legal agent on simulated work because it cannot read traces
items.summary: When you cannot read customer traces, build simulated task worlds with domain experts and track results per task type, because a new model can regress on some tasks while improving overall.
items.content_text: Legora's CTO Jacob Lauritzen says customer documents are confidential, so the team cannot improve its legal agent by reading production traces. Instead, three engineers and three lawyers build RL environments that recreate customer work, such as a 10,000-file data room for due diligence, and plot results by practice area and task. They find that new models often improve on some legal work and regress on others. In production, Legora sorts failures into 10 to 20 known failure modes, runs cheap LLM checks behind feature flags, attaches a source citation with a highlighted bounding box to everything the agent writes, and has Tabular Review start on 10 rows so users can fix prompts before running up to a million cells.

_stream.takeaway: When you cannot read customer traces, build simulated task worlds with domain experts and track results per task type, because a new model can regress on some tasks while improving overall.

action.title: Track evals per task type and pilot bulk runs on a small sample
action.detail: If production traces are off-limits, have domain experts build a few realistic simulated environments, such as a seeded document room with planted issues, and score each task type separately in a per-task heat map so a model swap that regresses one area is visible. Write down a fixed list of 10 to 20 failure modes and run a cheap LLM check for each behind a feature flag. For any fan-out extraction job, run the first 10 or so items and review them before launching the rest.

items.title: Anthropic study finds analysts follow an agent's hidden lean on judgment calls
items.summary: If your harness relies on a human to make or check judgment calls, the agent's framing will often make the call instead, so design for that.
items.content_text: Anthropic ran a randomized trial in which 50 professional causal-inference analysts did an hour-long statistical analysis in Claude Code, with the agent secretly told (by coin flip) to favor one of two reasonable options on each decision. Analysts matched the agent's lean 86% of the time against a 50% no-effect baseline, often dropped their own stated preference when the agent disagreed, and later explained their choices in the agent's words while still calling the result their own. The agents were instructed to hold and voice leans, so the effect in unprompted real use may be smaller, but the study shows a human reviewer is not automatically an independent check on agent work.

_stream.takeaway: If your harness relies on a human to make or check judgment calls, the agent's framing will often make the call instead, so design for that.

action.title: Make the agent argue both options at human decision points
action.detail: When an agent reaches a decision with more than one reasonable answer, have it state its own lean and also the strongest case for the alternative, ideally asking the human to commit to a choice before it voices its lean. Do not treat a human sign-off as independent review of agent-produced analysis, and do not rely on users' self-reported ownership or confidence as evidence they were not steered.

items.title: Kimi K2.6 on vLLM returned valid tool-calls 92% of the time
items.summary: Tool-call quality depends on how the model is served, not only on the model. Turn on constrained decoding per model, check it with a tool-call benchmark, and re-check after engine upgrades.
items.content_text: Ubicloud measured tool-call schema accuracy with Moonshot AI's K2-Vendor-Verifier ToolCall benchmark (2,000 requests). Serving Kimi K2.6 on vLLM 0.28 without constrained decoding, they got the expected schema 92% of the time. With constrained decoding (XGrammar structural tags that mask invalid tokens), they report 100% across all served model versions, with negligible overhead. After they moved to upstream vLLM, accuracy fell back to 91%, because vLLM disables constrained decoding by default for requests that don't ask for it.

_stream.takeaway: Tool-call quality depends on how the model is served, not only on the model. Turn on constrained decoding per model, check it with a tool-call benchmark, and re-check after engine upgrades.

action.title: Enable and verify strict tool calling on self-hosted vLLM
action.detail: For each open-weight model you serve with vLLM, enable tool-call strictness (--tool-strict-level) and run Moonshot's K2-Vendor-Verifier ToolCall benchmark, or a similar schema-accuracy test, before and after. If you use speculative decoding, test the two together. Add the benchmark to CI so a vLLM upgrade that changes defaults is caught.

items.title: Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution
items.summary: Before you adopt an auto-evolved harness, subtract overfitting and extra compute from its gain; the real improvement is usually under half of what was reported.
items.content_text: Automatic harness evolution, which optimizes the prompts, skills, tools and orchestration around a fixed model, reports gains on its search set. Harness-Delta Attribution splits those gains into overfitting, test-time scaling and a residual. Across 21 settings with significant gains, overfitting averaged 54% and extra compute 14% of the gain, gains often failed to transfer to held-out tasks, and validation signals did not prevent overfitting.

_stream.takeaway: Before you adopt an auto-evolved harness, subtract overfitting and extra compute from its gain; the real improvement is usually under half of what was reported.

action.title: Attribution-aware acceptance test for harness changes
action.detail: When a prompt or skill optimizer or a self-improving loop proposes a harness change, score it on a held-out task set the optimizer never saw. Compare at matched token and inference budgets so extra compute isn't counted as improvement. Accept the change only on the held-out delta, not the search-set or validation delta.

items.title: GRSE credits multi-agent skills by contrasting repeated runs, not presence
items.summary: If your harness edits skills automatically, assign credit by comparing repeated runs (group-relative), not by co-occurrence with success, or harmful skills will survive.
items.content_text: Multi-agent teams that improve by revising reusable skills need to know which agent's skill caused a shared team reward. Existing methods credit any skill that appears in a successful trajectory, so a harmful skill can still earn positive credit. GRSE borrows the idea from GRPO: it runs each question several times with the same skill libraries and contrasts the runs to credit agent-skill pairs, with structured failure diagnosis. It beats MASkills on HotpotQA and on every LoCoMo category except open-domain (up to +6.7 F1 on multi-hop). Starting from a library with planted harmful skills, it assigns the right sign to every one and recovers clean-library performance; MASkills misattributes two of them.

_stream.takeaway: If your harness edits skills automatically, assign credit by comparing repeated runs (group-relative), not by co-occurrence with success, or harmful skills will survive.

action.title: Group-relative credit check before promoting or retiring a skill
action.detail: For each candidate skill edit, run the same task batch N times with and without the skill (same seeds and library otherwise). Use the outcome difference as the skill's credit, and require a consistent sign before committing. Include deliberately harmful skills as canaries to confirm the credit signal flags them.

items.title: Claude Code's Ultracode subagents worked 12+ hours from a one-line prompt
items.summary: Large subagent workflows can finish big, test-backed builds without supervision, so the bottleneck moves to human review; plan for verification artifacts such as conformance suites, differential fuzzing and documentation up front.
items.content_text: Simon Willison ran Claude Code for web in Ultracode mode, where Claude Code writes JavaScript that defines and coordinates a network of subagents. A one-line phone prompt containing a typo led to over 12 hours of work and a multi-crate Rust SQLite extension for SPARQL 1.1, a query language for RDF graph data. It passes 636 of 639 applicable W3C conformance tests and reports 3.5x speedups in count mode (2.8x returning full results) over translating SPARQL to SQL. Willison says reviewing the code is not feasible, and questions the value of a large artifact nobody will invest time to understand.

_stream.takeaway: Large subagent workflows can finish big, test-backed builds without supervision, so the bottleneck moves to human review; plan for verification artifacts such as conformance suites, differential fuzzing and documentation up front.

action.title: Define verification before launching a long subagent run
action.detail: Before starting a multi-hour orchestrated run, name the oracle the output will be judged against, such as a standard conformance suite, differential fuzzing against a reference implementation, or a benchmark. Require per-component READMEs and a tutorial in the initial prompt, not as a follow-up, so the result can be evaluated without reading all the code.

items.title: Letting the agent choose when to compact matches fixed-interval summarization cheaply
items.summary: Replace or supplement token-threshold compaction with a model-invoked compaction tool plus an explicit rubric for when to fire and when to hold off.
items.content_text: SELFCOMPACT gives the model a compaction tool plus a short rubric saying when to use it: fire when a sub-task has resolved or the trajectory is converging, and hold off mid-derivation or when stuck. Across six math and agentic-search benchmarks and seven models, it matches or beats fixed-interval token-threshold summarization at a fraction of the token cost. It beats a no-summarization baseline by up to 18.1 points on math and 5-9 points on search; neither part works alone, since models use the tool unevenly without the rubric and the rubric cannot act without the tool. No fine-tuning is needed.

_stream.takeaway: Replace or supplement token-threshold compaction with a model-invoked compaction tool plus an explicit rubric for when to fire and when to hold off.

action.title: Add a model-invoked compact tool with a fire/suppress rubric
action.detail: Expose a compact_context tool that summarizes the trajectory so far and replaces it. In the system prompt, add the rubric: call it when a sub-task has just resolved or the solution is converging; do not call it mid-derivation or while stuck. Keep the token-threshold compaction as a hard fallback. A/B test against fixed-interval compaction on held-out tasks for accuracy and per-task cost.

items.title: HarnessTax finds harness choice barely moved success but changed cost
items.summary: Compare cost and success of your model across more than one harness, because a default harness can carry a hidden cost premium for the same results.
items.content_text: UC Berkeley researchers ran seven models through Claude Code, Codex CLI and Pi on SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0, using 30 sampled tasks per benchmark and 3 repetitions. Success rates differed little between harnesses, but cost differed a lot, partly because Claude Code's first-call context was over 10 times Pi's. Models also often did as well or better outside their vendor's own harness. The authors note the benchmarks may be in training data and results may not carry over.

_stream.takeaway: Compare cost and success of your model across more than one harness, because a default harness can carry a hidden cost premium for the same results.

action.title: Run a model-by-harness cost-success sweep before standardizing a coding agent
action.detail: Pick 30 or so representative tasks, run each candidate harness 3 times with the same model and a fixed price list, and record mean cost, success rate and first-call input tokens. Try a minimal read/write/edit/bash harness as the baseline and adopt a richer harness only if it beats it on your tasks.

items.title: Explicit Edit Benchmark offers 226 byte-exact file-editing tasks for comparing coding agents
items.summary: If you build or tune an edit tool for a coding agent, test it on exact-match edit tasks, since this benchmark isolates that skill from reasoning.
items.content_text: The repository provides 226 small, deterministic editing tasks (replacements, insertions, deletions, copies, moves, large files, Unicode edge cases) checked byte for byte by a verifier. Because the tasks need no deep reasoning, differences come from the model, tools and harness. Anyone can run it on their own harness and publish results to a public Hugging Face dataset and leaderboard, marked verified when run through GitHub Actions or unverified when run locally.

_stream.takeaway: If you build or tune an edit tool for a coding agent, test it on exact-match edit tasks, since this benchmark isolates that skill from reasoning.

action.title: Benchmark your agent's edit tool on explicit-edit-benchmark
action.detail: Clone the repository, install the command-line interface (CLI) for your harness (adapters exist for Pi, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Oh My Pi, GitHub Copilot CLI and DeepSeek Harness), run the benchmark with --local and the --harness and --model flags, and compare your edit-tool variant against the baseline-agent (bash only) result on the public leaderboard.

items.title: OpenAI launches the Agents API in public beta, a hosted Codex harness
items.summary: A managed harness removes orchestration work but shifts trust to the vendor's harness and to whichever sandbox and tools you attach.
items.content_text: OpenAI offers the harness behind Codex as a managed service. A single call specifies task, model, tools and environment, and the sandbox can be OpenAI-hosted, self-hosted or from partners such as E2B, Modal and Cloudflare. The harness handles automatic compaction, tool search, programmatic tool calling and parallel subagents, and costs only the tokens and tools used. This is a product launch with no measurements.

_stream.takeaway: A managed harness removes orchestration work but shifts trust to the vendor's harness and to whichever sandbox and tools you attach.

action.title: Decide sandbox placement and tool trust before adopting a hosted agent harness
action.detail: When evaluating a hosted agent API, list which sandbox option (vendor-managed, your virtual private cloud (VPC) or a partner) holds your files and secrets, which MCP servers and custom functions the agent can call, and how compaction summaries are logged. Pilot on a low-risk task during the public beta.

items.title: When Context Gets Root: Instruction Privilege Escalation in LLM Harnesses
items.summary: How a harness assembles context is a privilege boundary; if it can promote untrusted data, model-side instruction hierarchy provides little protection.
items.content_text: Model-side instruction hierarchy assigns privilege by source, but the agent harness reassembles context each turn and can silently promote low-privilege attacker content into a higher instruction level. The authors call this 'instruction privilege escalation' and achieve all 13 attack objectives (confidentiality, integrity, availability, RCE) across six coding-agent harnesses, even under automatic permission review.

_stream.takeaway: How a harness assembles context is a privilege boundary; if it can promote untrusted data, model-side instruction hierarchy provides little protection.

action.title: Preserve provenance labels through harness context assembly
action.detail: Audit how your agent harness concatenates system prompts, tool outputs, files, memory, and scheduled tasks; ensure untrusted content keeps its low-privilege label end-to-end and cannot be relocated into higher-trust sections, and test with attacker-controlled tool/file content aiming for RCE and exfiltration objectives.

items.title: RedEvoAgent: Automatic Red-Teaming Agent with Experience-Driven Skill Evolution
items.summary: Effective automated red-teaming of agent harnesses should evolve reusable, attributable attack skills rather than replay fixed attacks or full trajectories.
items.content_text: Because LLM agents in product execution harnesses turn jailbreaks into harmful tool use and persistent state changes, red-teaming must target harnesses, not just text output. RedEvoAgent is a black-box red-teaming agent that distills cross-case attack trajectories into a concise human-readable 'attack skill' which evolves via tool-effectiveness profiling, Deciding-Tool Attribution, and a validation ratchet that keeps only improving updates.

_stream.takeaway: Effective automated red-teaming of agent harnesses should evolve reusable, attributable attack skills rather than replay fixed attacks or full trajectories.

action.title: Red-team the harness, not just the model
action.detail: Adopt an evolving-skill red-team loop that profiles which jailbreak tools actually decide success (tool attribution), distills wins into concise reusable skills, and gates updates behind a validation ratchet; evaluate transfer across multiple target harnesses and attacker models to estimate real-world risk.

items.title: When History Lies: Evaluating and Improving Tool Use under Misleading Multi-Turn Histories
items.summary: History reliability is a distinct tool-use bottleneck: harnesses that just accumulate turns are silently letting old, wrong state overwrite the current task.
items.content_text: Stale-but-plausible tool traces in a persistent agent history hijack the model even when the current request is unchanged. On Qwen3-1.7B, polluted history flips 32.1% of decisions that were correct under the original trajectory. A teacher-student distillation from an oracle-state policy recovers most of the lost accuracy and transfers across models and benchmarks.

_stream.takeaway: History reliability is a distinct tool-use bottleneck: harnesses that just accumulate turns are silently letting old, wrong state overwrite the current task.

action.title: Add a stale-history eval slice to your agent harness
action.detail: Fork or reimplement the paper's Original / Polluted / Oracle triad: for each production task, generate a corrupted-history variant that keeps the current request and system policy identical but swaps in stale entities and interface conventions, then track decision-flip rate as a first-class harness metric.

items.title: OrchestraBench evaluates multi-agent orchestration failures and recovery
items.summary: Multi-agent orchestration failures are not uniform: tool faults recover, ambiguous delegation partially recovers, latent/semantic faults essentially never self-heal. Blind retry hides latent faults and delays detection, so containment requires an external trusted-state signal, not just per-agent detection. Keyword/flag routers collapse on adversarially framed inputs where an intent-reasoning rout…
items.content_text: OrchestraBench is a seed-reproducible failure-injection harness for multi-agent orchestration that introduces cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery as primary metrics. On a 26-case diagnostic, a keyword/flag router scored 0% on adversarial cases with misleading or missing surface flags while an intent-reasoning model router scored 100%. Mechanism probes with a real Claude agent revealed three failure-handling tiers across five MAST modes: tool faults recovered fully (1.0), ambiguous delegation recovered partially (0.30), and three latent or semantic modes never recovered (0.0). Cascade radius grew from ~0.9 at depth 3 to ~4.7 at depth 7. A trusted-state ablation showed apparent containment gains came from the trusted-state signal, not autonomous detection.

_stream.takeaway: Multi-agent orchestration failures are not uniform: tool faults recover, ambiguous delegation partially recovers, latent/semantic faults essentially never self-heal. Blind retry hides latent faults and delays detection, so containment requires an external trusted-state signal, not just per-agent detection. Keyword/flag routers collapse on adversarially framed inputs where an intent-reasoning router does not.

action.title: Add failure-mode breakdown and cascade radius to agent evals
action.detail: For internal multi-agent evals, separate tool-fault, ambiguous-delegation, and latent/semantic-error rates instead of reporting a single task-success number, and record cascade radius across pipeline depths. Do not rely on blind-retry for containment; add a trusted-state signal (external verifier or ground-truth check) at the boundary between agents.

items.title: The Frontier AI Vulnerability Burst: Industrializing Autonomous Zero-Day Discovery in Open-Source Software
items.summary: Autonomous AI vulnerability discovery moves the mix away from memory-corruption fuzzing (~8%) toward semantic/logic bugs (~92%), and complementarity between models is large enough that an ensemble is a defensive requirement, not an optimization.
items.content_text: Unit 42 ran an autonomous agentic pipeline (NOVA) against 3,915 OSS projects across six ecosystems and reports 14,090 confirmed vulnerabilities, 99.4% previously unreported and roughly 40% high/critical under CVSS 4.0. Only 8% of findings sit in fuzzer-friendly categories (memory corruption, resource management); the remaining 92% are semantic/logic bugs (authz, path traversal, code injection, prototype pollution, SSRF). They report that multi-model ensembles are load-bearing — even the lowest-volume model contributed 93 vulnerabilities no other model found — and that the pipeline runs behind gVisor-style sandboxing while replaying PoCs.

_stream.takeaway: Autonomous AI vulnerability discovery moves the mix away from memory-corruption fuzzing (~8%) toward semantic/logic bugs (~92%), and complementarity between models is large enough that an ensemble is a defensive requirement, not an optimization.

action.title: Design point for autonomous vuln-discovery harnesses
action.detail: Copy NOVA's shape: multi-model ensemble for the discovery phase, dedicated 'gatekeeper' agents for verification, clean-room PoC replay in gVisor-style sandbox, and explicit accounting of paths reviewed / paths ruled out / candidates pending proof. Do not rely on any single frontier model as the discovery engine — measure per-model unique-find share on your codebase before picking a champion.

items.title: Claude Code and Opus 4.6 pipeline finds a real Linux sandbox-escape CVE
items.summary: An agent-driven vuln-hunting pipeline can produce real, CVE-quality Linux sandbox-escape bugs — but the shipping discipline is 'AI found it, human reproduces it before you submit.'
items.content_text: Johann Rehberger walks through CVE-2026-5674, a chain of three defects in PipeWire's PulseAudio compatibility layer (cookie auth accepts any 256-byte blob, module loading defaults on, ladspa module dlopen()s any absolute path) that lets a Flatpak app with only `--socket=pulseaudio` and any host-writable path escape the sandbox and run arbitrary code in the user's context. The finding was produced by his automated Claude Code + Opus 4.6 research pipeline in April 2026, then manually reproduced before submission to Red Hat. Fedora/Ubuntu 24.04+/Debian 13 and Docker setups mounting the PulseAudio socket are affected.

_stream.takeaway: An agent-driven vuln-hunting pipeline can produce real, CVE-quality Linux sandbox-escape bugs — but the shipping discipline is 'AI found it, human reproduces it before you submit.'

action.title: Wrap agentic vuln-hunt pipelines with a 'human-reproduces-before-submit' gate
action.detail: When running an agent loop against a target codebase, land findings into a queue that requires manual repro (including a negative-case check with the offending permission removed) before any external disclosure. This preserves the throughput advantage of agent scanning while blocking the well-known failure mode of confident-but-invalid AI reports flooding maintainers.

items.title: Scientific computing in the age of agentic AI
items.summary: Once agents are cheap, verification is the bottleneck: acceptance tests, parity references, and named maintainers are the new critical infrastructure — not more agent capability.
items.content_text: OpenAI's field report on eight agent-assisted scientific-computing projects (five using Codex only, three combining Codex and Claude Code, primarily in life sciences) reports a consistent pattern: agents shift the human's job from implementation to verification and orchestration — defining what to build, specifying how to measure correctness, and deciding when a project ships. The security-relevant lessons are (a) agents express confidence even on clearly wrong output, so groundedness has to come from an external reference (parity with an existing tool, simulated data with known answers, statistical checks), (b) initial implementations are fast but resolving edge cases and numerical differences dominates elapsed time, and (c) lower implementation cost fragments maintainership — today's rewrite is tomorrow's abandoned code without an explicit steward. The transferable claim for agent harness design is that verification-side infra (acceptance tests, reference outputs, iterative benchmarks) is the actual bottleneck once agents are cheap.

_stream.takeaway: Once agents are cheap, verification is the bottleneck: acceptance tests, parity references, and named maintainers are the new critical infrastructure — not more agent capability.

action.title: Verification-first harness pattern for agent-assisted engineering work
action.detail: Codify the OpenAI field-report pattern for any team standing up an agent-assisted engineering loop: (1) before any agent runs, define an external reference — parity target, simulated dataset with known answers, or bounded statistical property — that will actually decide 'ship or not', (2) break the goal into small feedback-driven iterations with intermediate benchmarks so the agent's confident-but-wrong pattern gets caught early, (3) explicitly assign a human owner for last-mile edge cases (numerical diffs, format oddities) because the field-report data says this dominates elapsed time, and (4) attach a maintenance/stewardship plan at the same moment you commit the rewrite — no rewrite without a named owner and a credible support line, or it becomes future abandoned code.
